newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK airport authority defends fees for new airport.
newsitem.headline: HK airport authority defends fees for new airport.

text.p: Hong Kong's airport authority on Tuesday defended the charges it plans to levy on use of the territory's future Chek Lap Kok airport, arguing they were "fair, reasonable and competitive".
Hitting back at airlines which have criticised the planned charges as too expensive, senior officials also said it was unlikely that the planned fees would be re-adjusted.
"I don't see a great deal of scope for radical change... although we would be open to views," said Clinton Leeks, corporate development director, at a news conference.
"To ask us to lower our charges below a prudent commercial level would be the same as asking us for a subsidy, which we will not and cannot provide," he said.
Leeks also said the authority had held discussions with experts and airlines and conducted comparative studies of other major airports in the world before arriving at the figures.

Fees for passenger 747-type aircraft were planned at HK$66,877, or more than twice the HK$31,426 now charged at Kai Tak airport, while the 737-type aircraft would be charged HK$15,943 from the current HK$8,502.
The fees, which cover landing, parking and passenger charges, also put Chek Lap Kok in the mid-range of a group of 20 airports all over the world, the officials said.
The planned charges, to be approved by the government before they are formally announced around end September 1997, will be in force for a year after the airport opens in April 1998.
Leeks also said the increases were necessary as the airport, built at a cost of HK$49.8 billion, needed to repay loans and pay dividends to Hong Kong taxpayers.
"The charges will fulfil our obligations...namely to repay our borrowings and be able to pay a dividend to our owner, the Hong Kong taxpayer, by 2001," he said.
